opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that token efficiency is becoming one of the most important problems in pretraining. High-quality data on the internet is finite, so the question is no longer just how much compute you can throw at the problem, but how much intelligence you can extract from each token. If you can get the same loss with fewer tokens, that's effectively like expanding your data supply, and that compounds over time.

Muon is interesting because it attacks this from the optimizer side, which is a bit underexplored. For many years, almost everyone has just used Adam or AdamW as the default, and people focused on architecture or data. But Muon takes a different view of the update: instead of treating each parameter element independently, it looks at the weight matrix as a whole and orthogonalizes the update, so the update is spread more evenly across different directions rather than being dominated by a few large singular directions. Intuitively, that means each step is learning more "useful" structure, and empirically we saw it could be roughly twice as token-efficient as AdamW in our experiments.

But the interesting part is that it didn't just work out of the box at scale. When we scaled it up, we ran into issues like the attention logits blowing up, which caused training instability. So we had to do quite a lot of work, adding weight decay, adjusting the update scale to match Adam's, and eventually developing what we call QK-Clip to control the growth of the query-key logits. That's how we got to MuonClip, which let us train Kimi K2 at trillion-parameter scale with essentially no loss spikes.

So for me it's interesting on two levels. One is the practical level: it gives you a real multiplier on token efficiency, which matters a lot when data is the bottleneck. The other is more philosophical: it shows that there are still very fundamental components in the training stack that people assumed were solved, but actually have a lot of room for improvement. If you're willing to question those defaults and do the hard engineering to make them stable at scale, you can find gains that are pretty significant.

r001.rationale: The response says Muon treats the weight matrix as a whole and orthogonalizes its update, spreading learning across directions instead of treating parameter elements independently.

r002.rationale: It reports roughly twice the token efficiency in experiments, but does not say these were early experiments under compute-optimal conditions, and names AdamW rather than Adam.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think the simplest way to put it is this: in the end, the whole game is about turning compute into intelligence as efficiently as possible, and token efficiency is one of the biggest levers we have left. Pre-training is hitting a data wall. High-quality tokens are finite, and we can't just keep multiplying the data by ten. So if you can't get more tokens, the question becomes: how much more can you learn from each token you already have? That's exactly where the optimizer sits.

For a long time everyone just used AdamW. It's been the default for almost a decade, and it became kind of invisible, like nobody questioned it. But if you look at the structure of a transformer, most of the parameters are matrices, and Adam treats every element of a matrix independently. It doesn't really know it's optimizing a matrix. Muon takes a different view. It does an orthogonalization step on the update, so the update direction uses all the singular directions of the gradient more evenly, instead of letting a few dominant directions swallow everything. Intuitively, you're exploring the parameter space more fully per step, and that shows up as learning more from the same data.

When we started testing it, the early results on small models were already promising, roughly on the order of doubling the compute efficiency in some settings. But what made it interesting to me rather than just a nice paper result was whether it could scale. A lot of optimizer ideas look great at a hundred million parameters and then fall apart. We had to solve a few things, like adding proper weight decay and controlling the update scale so it was consistent with Adam, and once we did that we trained a trillion-parameter-scale MoE with it, and the gains held. That was the moment it became more than an academic curiosity.

The other reason it matters to me is more strategic. We're a smaller team with less compute than the biggest labs, so we can't win by brute force. Our only path is to be more efficient per unit of compute and per token. If the optimizer gives you a free multiplier on both, you'd be crazy not to take it. And honestly, I also just like that it's a case where first principles thinking paid off. Everyone assumed the optimizer was solved, and it turns out there was still a lot on the table.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Adam’s element-by-element treatment with Muon’s matrix-level approach and says its update uses singular directions more evenly, attributing greater learning per token to that mechanism.

r002.rationale: It reports roughly doubled compute efficiency in some early small-model settings, but does not say the experiments were compute-optimal or that Muon achieved twice Adam’s token efficiency.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting about Muon is that it changes how effectively the model learns from each batch of tokens. It takes the momentum update for a weight matrix and approximately orthogonalizes it, which changes the balance between directions in the update rather than just rescaling individual parameters.

The hope is that this lets you reach the same loss with fewer training tokens. If that holds, you can spend the same data budget and get a better model, or reach a target capability with less training. But I’d distinguish token efficiency from compute efficiency: the optimizer adds some work, so the practical question is whether the reduction in training steps outweighs that overhead. That’s what makes it an interesting direction to test.

r001.rationale: The response describes orthogonalizing a matrix update and balancing update directions, but does not attribute improved learning efficiency to considering dependencies among matrix parameters.

sol-6.1.text:
I find Muon interesting because token efficiency isn’t only about choosing better data. It’s also about how much progress the model makes from each token it sees. If an optimizer gets us to the same loss with fewer training tokens, that’s a meaningful efficiency gain.

Muon changes how we update weight matrices. It approximately orthogonalizes the momentum, which can keep the update from being dominated by just a few directions. The intuition is that you can make progress across more directions in the parameter space, rather than repeatedly emphasizing the strongest ones.

Of course, the important question is whether that translates into better results at a fixed compute budget. You have to account for the optimizer’s overhead and check downstream performance, not just training loss. But improving how effectively we learn from the tokens we already have is a very attractive direction.
